title: A melt-energy threshold on days above 0 C gave most of the missing melt-start and peak-SWE effects on SNOTEL melt rates in 1988-2025; cloud, humidity and wind anomalies added little
abstract: An earlier campaign result (sci:24cc0799) showed that earlier and smaller snowpacks melt more slowly at SNOTEL stations, but a temperature-radiation index model gave only 70% of the melt-start slope and 49% of the peak-SWE elasticity. We tested causes with daily NASA POWER shortwave, longwave, humidity and wind at each station. We used 22,098 melt seasons at 721 stations in water years 1988-2025 and constant station parameters fitted to daily SWE loss. We reproduced the earlier seasons and shares exactly. Measured shortwave, snow-age albedo, humidity, wind and sensible heat raised the shares only to 73% and 59%. One constant energy loss on days above 0 C (a melt threshold) raised them to 108% (95% station-bootstrap CI 106-110%) and 86% (84-89%) with TOA radiation, and to 103% and 84% with the shortwave climatology. Parameters from the other half of the years gave the same shares. A degree-day model with a fitted base temperature gave only 58% and 42%. The threshold result held in all 12 states with 10 or more stations, in Alaska, with year fixed effects and in low-precipitation seasons. After the threshold, daily weather anomalies did not change the shares (100% and 86%). The median threshold is approximately 90-120 W m-2, near the net longwave loss of melting snow. Thus the slower melt of early and small snowpacks is mainly a seasonal energy effect with a loss term, which linear index models underestimate. About 14% of the peak-SWE elasticity remains, partly related to snowfall during melt. Limitations: the threshold models were added after the first run, POWER grids are 0.5-1 degree, and the threshold is an effective parameter.

display.caption: Within-station slopes of log melt rate on melt start (left) and log peak SWE (right) for observed data and 11 index models in the same 22,098 seasons (95% CI, two-way clustered). Grey: models without a threshold; blue: models with a constant energy term on days above 0 C. Orange squares: parameters fitted on the other half of the years. Percentages are shares of the observed slope.

Left and centre: binned within-station relations of log melt rate to log peak SWE (melt start held fixed) and to melt start (peak SWE held fixed), observed and for the temperature + TOA radiation model with and without a threshold. Right: observed and model slopes in 12 states with 10 or more stations.

Seasonal shape of daily melt for median fitted parameters at 42 N and a fixed 3 C mean temperature, relative to 1 May. With the threshold, the melt energy increases much faster through spring. Illustration only.
